rule: Symmetric subjects such as buildings and faces need precise construction; only naturally asymmetric subjects tolerate free variation in proportion and line.
A form's lit edge can be left with no outline at all; the shadow side alone defines the edge and the viewer supplies the rest.
Minimise outlines in the finished drawing; define forms through tone and shadow rather than contour lines.
Where one element passes in front of another, leave a small gap so the lines do not touch; touching lines destroy the illusion of depth.
Put the greatest contrast and finest detail where the viewer's attention should go.
Suggest detail rather than render all of it; adequate suggestion lets the viewer complete the rest.
Excluding detail from a face gives the impression of bright light flooding it.
Hatch marks curve to describe concave or convex surfaces and run straight on flat ones.
Fog and haze reduce distant objects to flat monotone silhouettes; only near objects keep tonal gradation.
Alternate light and dark masses to separate successive planes and show distance.
Check a drawing in a mirror to expose proportion and perspective errors before finishing.
Build dark tones from light to dark in layers, keeping the first light layer where highlights belong.
